_readme: What somebody standing in a shop should actually buy, and what it should cost.
THE READER IS A PARENT IN AN AISLE, or somebody who has just decided to get
into this, holding a phone, looking at a wall of boxes between nine dollars
and four hundred. They do not know what an ETB is. They do not know why one
box is $10 and another is $180. They do not know that the $300 booster box on
a big retailer's website is somebody else's listing rather than the shop's.
Tim ends up explaining this in shops, out loud, to strangers. This is that
conversation.
THIS FILE HOLDS NO PRICES AND MUST NEVER HOLD ONE. Every figure the page
prints is joined out of data/msrp.json by the exact `label` string, and every
pack count out of data/pack-counts-current.json through that row's
`packsFrom`. A label this file names that msrp.json does not carry FAILS THE
BUILD, and so does a `pick` pointing at a row with no sourced price. That is
the whole point of naming products instead of describing them: /msrp.html and
this page cannot print different numbers for the same box, and the day
somebody re-reads a source and edits msrp.json, this page moves with it or
stops the build.
IT HOLDS NO PRODUCT DESCRIPTIONS EITHER. The sentence saying what a thing IS
comes from that row's `what` in msrp.json, for the same reason. What this file
owns is WHY somebody would buy it, in the second person, which is the only
part /msrp.html has no business carrying: that page is a price list and this
one is a recommendation.
NO PULL RATES, NO ODDS, NO INVESTMENT. Site-wide rule and it bites hardest
here, because a page advising a parent is exactly where 'and it might be worth
something one day' wants to creep in. Nothing here says what is in a pack, how
likely anything is, or that any of it is worth buying as anything other than a
thing to open and play with. Do not add a sentence about holding sealed.
NO GATEKEEPING, AND IT IS THE OPERATIVE WORD. Never write a sentence that
makes a reader feel stupid for not knowing a word. Every piece of jargon gets
its plain-English meaning in the same breath, the first time, every time. If a
sentence would make somebody put their phone away rather than ask, rewrite it.
situations[]   the six shapes of person who asks. Each has:
id           an anchor, kebab case
who          the headline, in the reader's own words
sub          the situation, so somebody can recognise themselves in it
picks[]      { product, why } where `product` is an exact msrp.json label
and `why` is one or two sentences of second-person reason.
The product must carry a sourced price. First pick is the
recommendation, later ones are the alternative.
links[]      [href, label] internal cross references, optional
quick[]        the three-line strip at the very top, above everything. Exact
msrp.json labels plus a `for` clause of about six words. THESE
ARE THE FIRST CONCRETE RECOMMENDATIONS ON THE PAGE AND THEY
HAVE TO CLEAR THE FOLD ON A 390px PHONE, which is why they
carry no photograph and no more than one clause each. Anything
added to a row here comes out of that budget. Measured.
glossary[]     { product, plain } where `plain` is the beginner gloss in this
page's voice. The formal description comes from msrp.json's own
`what` and is printed under it. Ordered smallest to biggest,
deliberately: a shelf reads left to right and a beginner meets
the pack before the box.
avoid[]        { title, body[], product? }. `product` names an msrp.json row
so the section can print the suggested figure it is arguing
about. body is paragraphs; the builder does the arithmetic.
reseller       the marketplace section. `evidence` is NOT written here: the
builder reads data/buying.json, which already records each
chain's own return and shipping pages with the url and the day
they were read, and pulls the marketplace lines out of it. Do
not paste a claim about a retailer in here.
counter        the ask-an-employee section. No claim about any named shop.
playing        which products contain a deck you can actually play with.
`products` are msrp.json labels; the page prints them with
their prices and links /how-to-play.html.
collector      THE ONE BLOCK ON THIS PAGE THAT IS NOT FOR A BEGINNER, and it
is the only reason it is worth its length. Every situation
above assumes the RECIPIENT is new. This block assumes the
recipient knows far more than the buyer does, which inverts
the whole problem: the risk stops being 'is this any good'
and becomes 'do they already have it' and 'will they think
this is junk'. The buyer cannot ask without spoiling it and
has never seen the collection.
IT SITS DIRECTLY AFTER `oneCard` BECAUSE THE TWO WOULD
OTHERWISE CONTRADICT EACH OTHER. oneCard says buy the card
rather than packs. This block says a single card is the
worst blind gift there is. Both are true and the difference
is whether you KNOW which card, so the two are printed next
to each other and each names the other. Do not move one
without moving the other.
Fields:
id        the anchor
title     the h2
lede      one sentence under it
intro[]   the framing paragraphs
tests[]   {q, a} the three questions that decide whether a
gift is safe. This is the durable half: it works
on a product this page does not list.
safe[]    {product, why} exact msrp.json labels, ascending
by price. Each MUST carry a sourced price: the
builder prints a walk-away ceiling beside every
one and a ceiling with no price under it is
useless in a shop.
ceiling   {title, body[]} the copy around the computed
overpay figures. NO NUMBERS IN HERE. The builder
computes the multiple from data/over-msrp.json's
own bands and the evidence range from every dated
shop listing this repo holds.
supplies  {title, body[]} the accessories half. THIS REPO
HAS NO SOURCED PRICE FOR SLEEVES, TOPLOADERS OR A
PLAIN BINDER, because msrp.json is a list of
sealed Pokemon product and those are other
companies' goods. So this block names them and
prints no figure, and says so. Do not fix that by
typing one in.
unsafe[]  {title, body[], links[]} what not to give blind.
gaps[]    what this page could not source, in plain words.
links[]   [href, label] cross references
No em dashes anywhere in site copy. Second person. Short sentences. It is
allowed to be funny and it is not allowed to be clever at the reader's
expense.

quick.for: the cheap one that still feels like a present
when the fun is opening packs and nothing else
the big birthday box with everything in it

situations.who: A present for a young kid
situations.sub: Five, six, seven. They love Pokemon, they have never opened a pack, and they have definitely never played the game. You want the thing that will not confuse them.

picks.why: This is the one. It is built for somebody who has never played anything, it works straight out of the box with no rules to learn first, and it is the cheapest box on this page that comes with a game to play. A grown up can sit down with them and play it in about ten minutes.
If what they actually want is the opening bit, get this instead. Two packs, a promo card, and a tin they will still be keeping pencils in when they are fifteen.

situations.who: A kid who already collects and just wants to open stuff
situations.sub: They know what they are doing. They have a binder. What they want is more packs, and everything you hand them that is not a pack is going in a drawer.

picks.why: Packs and nothing else. No dice they will lose, no board they will not use, no sleeves they will not put on. At the suggested prices a pack in here costs exactly what a pack in the giant thirty six pack box costs, so this is the cheap way to buy packs without committing to a whole box.

The half sized version of the same idea, and the one that hangs on a peg where you can actually reach it. It has a promo card showing through the front, so there is one card they can see before you buy it.

situations.who: Somebody who wants to actually play the game
situations.sub: A kid whose friends play at school, or a grown up who has decided this year is the year. They need two decks and the rules, not a pile of loose cards.

picks.why: Three finished decks, a board, counters and a rulebook, and not a single booster pack, which is the entire point. You cannot learn this game out of booster packs, and almost everything else on that shelf is booster packs. Two people can open this and be playing in twenty minutes.

situations.who: A kid who already plays and wants a proper deck
situations.sub: They have played, they know what a Trainer card does, and the deck they built out of packs is sixty cards of chaos that loses to everything.

picks.why: A finished sixty card deck, built to be played, with the sleeves, dice and counters to play it. Open it, shuffle it, take it to a league night. Nothing to build and nothing missing.
The cheaper one. Smaller box, one big card at the centre of it, and still a real deck rather than a pile you have to finish yourself.

situations.who: The big present, one box with everything in it
situations.sub: Birthday, Christmas, end of a hard term. You want to hand over one box that is obviously A Present and not have to explain what any of it is.

picks.why: This is the birthday box and it is why everybody keeps saying those three letters at you. Packs to open, a lidded box to keep the cards in afterwards, sleeves so the good ones stop getting bent, dice and counters for when they start playing. It is the only product that covers the opening and the keeping and the playing in one go.

Pokemon's own version of the same box: a couple of extra packs and a stamped promo card you cannot get in the shop one. It costs a bit more and it has to be ordered rather than carried home, so it is a plan-ahead present rather than a Saturday one.

situations.sub: A stocking, a party bag, a reward for a decent report card, or just this is what there is this week. Nobody should feel bad about this bracket. It is where most of the fun is anyway.

picks.why: The best ten dollars on the shelf. Two packs, a promo card and a tin that survives a school bag. It also stacks, which matters more than you would think when there are four of them.

A few dollars more buys three packs and a promo card you can see through the front before you pay for it. Per pack it works out a shade above a bundle, and it is the smallest thing on the shelf that still unwraps like a proper present.

links: What a pack costs across every set

oneCard.title: They want one specific card
body: Then buy that card. Not packs. Somebody already opened the packs, and the card they want is sitting on a shelf somewhere with a price on it, which is a thing you can do in an afternoon instead of a thing you might do in a year.
It is one of the most expensive mistakes in the whole hobby and it gets made with the best intentions every single time.

collector.title: Buying for somebody who already collects
collector.lede: Everything above assumes the person opening it is new to this. This part is the opposite: they know far more than you do, and you have no idea what they already own.
intro: Somebody in your life is properly into Pokemon cards. You have never seen the collection, you cannot ask without ruining the surprise, and every box in the shop looks equally plausible.

The problem is not the one you think. You are not being asked to pick something good. You are being asked to pick something they do not already have and will not quietly think is a waste, which is a job you can actually do. So stop trying to guess their taste, because guessing is where this goes wrong, and pick something that leaves the choosing to them.

tests.q: Could they already have this exact thing?
tests.a: A sealed pack cannot be. Nobody knows what is inside one until it is opened, so there is no version of it already sitting in their binder. A specific card can be, and for anybody who has collected a while, the obvious cards usually are.

tests.q: Do they still get to decide something?
tests.a: Sealed product hands the choice over instead of making it for them: open it, keep it shut, trade it. The more serious the collector, the stronger their opinions about sealed against opened, this era against that one, graded against raw, and none of those are opinions you can guess.

tests.q: Is it from what is on the shelf right now?
tests.a: The current line is what everybody is opening this month, which makes it the least likely thing to land oddly. Buying something older blind means picking an era for somebody who has already picked their own.

safe.why: The small, safe, nobody-minds one. Two packs and a promo, and the tin itself is genuinely useful. If you are buying for a group, or you want something to go with a card you already bought, this is the one that never feels like a mistake.

Packs and nothing else, from whatever set is out now. This is the purest version of the whole idea: you are handing over the part they enjoy and none of the part you had to guess at. Somebody who has collected for ten years still has not opened these particular packs.

A ring binder with a few packs in it, and the only thing here that is half supplies. Every collector fills binders and then needs another one, and a spare binder is not a duplicate in a way that stings. It is the closest thing on the shelf to a gift that gets used every week.

The safest big one. Packs to open, plus sleeves, dice, counters and a box to keep cards in, and those bits get used on whatever they collect rather than on what you guessed they collect. It is also the product most likely to be marked up in a hurry, so check the number below before you pay.

ceiling.title: What to pay, and when to walk away
body: This is the part worth real money to you, because somebody buying a present is the most likely person in the shop to be asked too much and not know it. You are in a hurry, it is for somebody else, and you have no idea what any of this normally costs. So carry one number instead of a list, and work out the multiple before you pay it rather than after.

None of which means walk out on principle. A shop that has the thing on the shelf today, when four other places are sold out, has done something for you, and a bit over the suggested price is what that is worth. The point of the sum is that you are the one deciding.

supplies.title: The other safe answer is supplies
body: Sleeves, toploaders, a deck box, a binder. Every collector uses these up, everybody ends up short of them, and nobody has ever been annoyed to get more. They sidestep the duplicate problem entirely, because there is no such thing as a card you already own twice in plastic.

This site holds no sourced price for any of them, so no figure is printed here for a pack of sleeves: they are other companies' goods and the price list this page is built on covers sealed Pokemon product only. The Binder Collection above is the one that is both, which is why it has a number beside it. The safest version of the whole idea is supplies with a bundle on top. The supplies get used, the packs get opened, and neither one needed you to know their taste.

unsafe.title: Do not pick one specific card for them
body: This is the trap. It is what an outsider reaches for first because it looks like the personal option, and it is the least safe thing on the shelf. You are guessing three things at once: that they want that Pokemon, that they want that version of it, and that they do not already have it. A collector of any standing has the obvious cards. You also cannot judge condition from a photo on a screen, and condition is most of what a card is worth to somebody who cares.

If you actually know which card, that is a different situation and it is the one directly above this. Buy it, from somewhere with a returns policy. It is the guessing that is the problem, not the card.
links: When you do know the card

unsafe.title: Do not buy a graded card blind
body: A graded card is one card sealed in a plastic case with a company's number on it, and it cannot come out without destroying the grade. So you are choosing the card, the grade and the grading company on their behalf, permanently, for somebody who almost certainly has views on all three. Plenty of collectors want their cards raw, in a binder, where they can look at them.
It is also the easiest thing here to overpay on, because a graded card has no suggested price at all. There is nothing to divide by.

unsafe.title: Do not buy a mystery box or a repack
body: The full argument is further down this page and it applies double here. The short version is that nobody at Pokemon made it: somebody bought cards, chose what went in, sealed the bag and priced it. A collector will know instantly what it is, which makes this the one thing on this page that can actually land badly.

unsafe.title: Do not buy old sealed product blind
body: An unopened box from ten years ago looks like the impressive choice and is the riskiest thing here. Which era somebody collects is a real preference, and old sealed is exactly the purchase people make for themselves after thinking about it. It is also the one thing this page cannot help you check: the figures here are what the manufacturer suggests for what it currently sells, and nothing suggests a price for a box that went out of print. What an old box costs is set entirely by how few are left, so there is nothing to divide by.

And one thing worth saying plainly, because it is what sellers of this lean on. Nothing on this page is bought because it might be worth more later. It is a present. Buy it to be opened or to sit on a shelf, and let whatever happens to its value be somebody else's problem.
links: What old sealed actually goes for

gaps: It has no idea what any particular person owns and never will. Everything above reasons from what a product IS, not from anything measured about your collector, which is exactly why the three questions still work on a product this page does not list.

It holds no sourced price for sleeves, toploaders, deck boxes or a plain binder, so none is printed. Same for anything second hand, anything graded and any sealed product out of print, none of which has a suggested price to check an asking price against.
It holds no prices at all from any local card shop, because nobody has walked into one with a notebook. If you are standing in one, do the division yourself against the figures above.
links: Check any price against the list

glossary.plain: A booster pack. One sealed foil packet of cards. This is the atom: nearly everything else on the shelf is a box with some of these inside it, plus something extra, and the whole game of working out what a box is worth is counting the packs.

A blister. The plastic-fronted card that hangs on a peg, with packs behind it and usually a promo card and sometimes a coin showing through the front. Nobody outside the hobby has ever used the word blister for this and it is not your fault for not knowing it.
A tin. A small metal one, with packs and a promo inside. Tins come in about four sizes and the small one is the cheap one; the bigger tins hold more and cost more, and they are all just tins.
A bundle. A sleeve of packs, shrink wrapped, and genuinely nothing else in the box. If somebody says the word bundle at you, this is what they mean.

An ETB, and here is the thing nobody bothers to tell you: it is a cardboard box with a lid, with packs in it and the bits for looking after cards. Sleeves, dice, counters, a place to put them. That is the whole mystery. Everybody says ETB because saying Elite Trainer Box out loud takes too long.
The learn to play box, and the only thing here that is a board game rather than a pile of packs. If the goal is to play rather than to open, this is the shelf you want.
The prerelease box, which is a shop-event thing that also sells normally. It is the one product that is both: a deck you can play with today and packs to open on the way.

A booster box, sometimes called a display box, because it is the box a shop opens to fill the shelf you are standing at. Thirty six packs. This is the big one and there is a section below about why it is almost never the right first purchase.

avoid.title: Do not start with a booster box
body: It is the biggest thing on the shelf, so it looks like the serious purchase, and every restock video on the internet is somebody buying one. It is the wrong first buy for almost everybody and the reason is not the one people assume.

It is not a bulk discount. The arithmetic is below and it is the same price a pack either way, so what the big box actually buys you is thirty six packs at once, opened in one sitting, and then it is over. Two bundles across two months is the same packs and about six weeks more fun.
Buy one because you want to open thirty six packs on a Friday night. That is a real reason and it is a completely different reason from thinking it is the sensible way to buy.

avoid.title: Do not grab one pack off the peg by the till
body: Here is the surprise. The suggested price of one pack is exactly the same as the price of a pack inside a bundle or inside the giant box. On paper the single pack is not a rip off at all.

What happens in real life is that the markup lands hardest on the smallest thing, because a few dollars on a peg item is the amount nobody argues about. The one shop listing this site has written down for a single pack, below, was more than double the suggested figure, and it is the worst multiple of any listing on this site.

So the rule is not that packs are bad. It is that the impulse buy at the counter, with a kid pulling on your sleeve, is where you are least likely to check and most likely to pay double. Walk ten feet to the peg with the three-pack blister on it and check both.

avoid.title: Do not buy a mystery box or a repack
body: A mystery box, a mystery pack, a repack, a hundred cards with a guaranteed hit: none of these is a Pokemon product. The Pokemon Company does not make them. Somebody bought cards, chose which ones go in, sealed the bag themselves and priced it.

That is not automatically a scam and some are made by perfectly honest people. It is just that you are no longer buying a sealed product from the company that printed the cards, you are buying a stranger's judgement about what to put in a bag, and there is no way to check it from the outside.
The test is easy: if you cannot find the exact product in a shop that sells Pokemon, it is somebody's own creation. Every product on this page is one the manufacturer makes and sells itself.

reseller.title: The one thing almost nobody knows
reseller.lede: If you take one thing off this page, take this. It is worth more money to you than everything above it.
body: The big retailers' websites are two things wearing one page. They are the shop, selling the shop's own stock at the shop's own price, and they are also a marketplace, where other companies list their own goods on the same site and set their own prices.

So when the shop's own stock of a box sells out, the page does not go empty. It fills up with other people's listings of the same box, at whatever they feel like asking. The site looks identical. The logo is the same. The price is not.

That is why a box can show up at a genuinely shocking number on a website you have used for years, on a page that looks completely normal. The shop has not put its prices up. That is a stranger's price sitting on the shop's website.

The tell is printed on every listing and almost nobody reads it: look for who it is sold by and who ships it. If either line is a company name you have never heard of, you are buying from that company and not from the shop. The return window is usually shorter too, which is its own warning sign about who is actually on the hook.

What to do about it is boring and it works. Do not pay it. Stock comes back, usually weekly, and the shop's own price comes back with it. A box that is unavailable this week is still a box, and paying several times the suggested price for one because the page had a familiar logo on it is the most common way somebody new to this loses money.
links: Every venue, and what it costs a buyer

counter.title: An empty shelf does not mean no stock
body: Cards get stolen, so a lot of shops now keep them behind the counter, in a locked case, or in a back room, and put nothing at all in the aisle where they used to be. Plenty of people walk the empty aisle, decide there is none, and leave.

Ask somebody who works there. That is the whole trick. Ask if there is any Pokemon behind the counter, ask when the truck comes, ask what day they put it out. Nobody is going to laugh at you and most of them will just tell you.

The same goes for a proper card shop, where the good stuff is behind glass by definition. Walking in and saying you have no idea what you are doing and it is for a seven year old is a completely normal thing to say in a card shop, and it gets you better advice than any website including this one.

playing.title: If the point is to play the game
body: Most of the shelf does not contain a deck you can play with. Packs are loose cards, and a pile of loose cards is not a deck any more than a bucket of Lego is a spaceship. If somebody wants to play, you need a product that has finished decks in it, and there are only a few.

Everything else on this page is for opening and collecting, which is a completely valid thing to want. Just do not buy an Elite Trainer Box for somebody who asked to learn how to play and wonder why they are stuck.
